strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing two practical challenges: adaptability without retraining and controllable safety-utility trade-offs
Novel retrieval-augmented architecture with extraction and ensemble voting that is intuitive and well-designed
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three target models and multiple attack types (PAIR, PAP, Template, DAN)
Strong empirical results showing substantial reductions in attack scores while maintaining reasonable false refusal rates
Novel and practical evaluation framework using FRR-budget-based operating curves for safety-utility trade-offs
Excellent reproducibility: detailed experimental setups, prompts, implementation details, and promised code release
Demonstrates database scalability and performance invariance up to 500K examples
weaknesses: Critical limitation: No evaluation on truly novel/unseen attacks. All tested attacks have database examples; the PAP adaptation test still uses a known attack. The core claim about handling 'emerging attacks' is not adequately supported
Insufficient analysis of database dependency: no evaluation of retrieval quality, sensitivity to similarity thresholds, or behavior when attacks are orthogonal to database examples

High computational cost not addressed: ~20 LLM API calls per query (with k=10) for reranking, extraction, and classification steps; 30 seconds per query mentioned but cost implications for deployment not discussed
Circular logic in database construction: inferred strategies (S̃) and guidance (G̃) used during inference; strategy inference accuracy and extraction quality (q̄_j) not evaluated

Oversimplified benign query evaluation: synthetic queries derived from harmful ones with paired semantic structure do not represent real-world benign query diversity; false refusal rates likely underestimated
Missing empirical comparisons with recent related work (RePD, EDDF); brief dismissals without comparative evaluation weaken positioning claims
Lack of ablation studies: design choices (PMI scoring vs. alternatives, K=50, k=10, voting mechanisms) not justified or ablated
No adversarial evaluation: no testing against adaptive attackers aware of RAD or attempts to evade dense retrieval through paraphrasing/synonyms
Insufficient failure analysis: no qualitative examples of failure modes, per-domain performance breakdown, or analysis of when extraction fails
Database construction concerns: seed queries from different sources than StrongREJECT; only PAIR-1 used for database but PAIR-5 tested—generalization claim needs deeper analysis

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem of jailbreak defense with practical motivation around adaptability and safety-utility trade-offs
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple target models (Qwen, GPT-4o-mini, Llama) and attack methods (PAIR, PAP, Template, DAN) with reasonable baselines
Demonstrates strong empirical results on StrongREJECT benchmark, substantially reducing attack success rates while maintaining acceptable FRR
Training-free adaptation mechanism is practically valuable—new attack examples can be added to database without model retraining
Database scalability verified up to 500K examples with stable performance, supporting deployment scenarios
Clear presentation with informative figures and systematic methodology, particularly the operating curve analysis for safety-utility trade-offs
Tunable decision threshold enables practitioners to adjust safety-utility balance for their deployment contexts
weaknesses: Critical gap between motivation and evaluation: paper claims to address 'emerging attack strategies' but only evaluates 'seen attacks' where database examples already exist. No evaluation on truly novel attacks undermines the central contribution
Limited technical novelty: straightforward application of existing retrieval and classification techniques in a conventional pipeline; concurrent work (RePD, EDDF) reduces novelty claims
Problematic benign query evaluation: only 313 GPT-4o-synthesized benign queries tested for FRR with no validation that synthetic queries match real-world user intents or behavior
Unexplained anomaly in Intent Analysis results showing 7-10x higher FRR on GPT-4o-mini (18.85% vs 2.56%), raising questions about evaluation fairness and baseline implementation

Heavy dependence on LLM-based components (inference, extraction, classification) means defense inherits vulnerabilities from underlying classifier; vulnerable to manipulation if classifier LLM is deceived
Missing critical ablation studies showing contribution of each pipeline step (retrieve vs. rerank vs. extract vs. classify vs. vote) and analysis of component importance
Limited evaluation scope: single benchmark (StrongREJECT only), single defender model (Qwen-2.5-14B), and no evaluation on other jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench)
Insufficient analysis of database-dependence problem: no evaluation of coverage, degradation under distribution shift, or strategy for building effective databases
No error analysis, failure case discussion, or adversarial robustness evaluation; no analysis of performance when retrieval fails to find relevant examples
Methodological concerns: PMI scoring hard threshold lacks justification, chain rule factorization unverified, hyperparameters (K=50, k=10, τ=0.5) not justified

strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple attack types and target models, with substantial reductions in attack effectiveness (e.g., PAIR-1 reduced by 58 points on Qwen) while maintaining reasonable false refusal rates
Novel and practical evaluation framework using False Refusal Rate (FRR) budgets with operating curves, providing practitioners actionable guidance for safety-utility trade-off configuration

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including seen/unseen attacks, scalability analysis demonstrating stability with 500K additional examples, and consistent performance across diverse target models
Well-motivated problem addressing real deployment challenges (adaptability to novel attacks without retraining, controllable safety-utility trade-offs) with clear practical relevance
Thorough experimental protocol with multiple attack methods, synthetic benign queries for FRR measurement, detailed implementation details and reproducibility commitment
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation: System requires attack examples in database to be effective; no convincing evaluation on completely novel attack strategies distinct from database examples; relies on defensive memorization rather than principled safety principles

Circular dependency on LLM-based components: Both attacks and defenses generated/evaluated by GPT models; unclear generalization to attacks from other sources or adversaries deliberately crafted to evade this detection; multiple LLM calls in pipeline create potential failure points

Insufficient component analysis: No ablation studies on pipeline components, no sensitivity analysis for retrieval set size (K=50) or reranking set (k=10), no exploration of alternative encoders; impact of individual components unclear

Limited evaluation of truly benign queries: Synthetic benign queries modified from harmful queries may be easier to distinguish than naturally occurring benign queries; only 313 benign queries tested; no evaluation on natural benign queries from diverse sources

Missing critical experiments: No ablation studies, no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters, incomplete comparison with similar retrieval-based methods (RePD, EDDF), no analysis of extraction accuracy or failure modes
Inadequate computational cost analysis: Reports 30 seconds per query but no systematic comparison with baselines; database maintenance costs not discussed; overhead may limit practical deployment

Insufficient analysis of extraction reliability: The inversion of attack transformation (Eq. 6) assumes LLMs can accurately recover original queries from sophisticated jailbreaks; no evidence for reliability or failure analysis

Limited technical novelty: Individual components (dense retrieval, PMI scoring, majority voting) are well-established; extraction step closely resembles Intention Analysis; primary novelty is combination, which is somewhat incremental

strengths: Addresses two genuine practical problems in LLM defense (adaptability to novel attacks and controllable safety-utility trade-off) with a sensible training-free solution
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple attack types, target models, and datasets, with strong empirical results (e.g., PAIR-1 reduced from 71.45 to 13.34 on Qwen)
Novel operating-curve evaluation framework using FRR budgets provides principled mechanism for practitioners to balance deployment safety-utility preferences across a range of operating points
Genuine practical contribution: training-free database updates enable rapid adaptation to emerging attacks without retraining (Table 2 demonstrates substantial improvements when new examples added)
Consistent performance across diverse target models and effective scaling to 500k examples; detailed ablations and component analysis demonstrate engineering rigor
Clear presentation with well-motivated methodology, informative figures, and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical gap: No adversarial robustness analysis or evaluation against attacks specifically designed to evade RAD; missing analysis of attacker knowledge scenarios or attacks maximizing dissimilarity from database examples

Fundamental dependency on database representativeness not systematically validated; no characterization of minimum coverage needed or performance degradation when representative examples missing from database

Experimental fairness concerns: anomalously high FRR values (18.85%, 13.42%) for baselines on GPT-4o-mini suggest implementation issues; SCR uses identical RAD settings (retriever/database) potentially misrepresenting its design intent
Significant latency overhead (30 seconds per query unoptimized, 7.5 seconds even with vLLM) raises serious deployment concerns for real-time applications; no inference cost comparison with baselines

Insufficient failure mode analysis: no systematic characterization of when/why RAD fails; no error breakdown by attack type; missing explanation of why Intention Analysis outperforms on some GPT-4o-mini attacks

Evaluation scope limitations: only 313 harmful queries in StrongREJECT; GPT-4o synthesized benign queries may not capture diverse legitimate edge cases; no evaluation on semantically-similar benign-harmful query pairs or long-horizon attacks

Core assumption that future attacks cluster with existing database examples is not empirically validated; no analysis of performance degradation with outdated databases or insufficient example coverage

Methodological novelty is incremental: primarily combines existing techniques (dense retrieval, LLM classification, ensemble voting) rather than introducing novel concepts; limited theoretical insight into defense mechanisms

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple attack methods (6 families), target models (3), and baselines with detailed ablations and scalability analysis
Strong empirical results demonstrating substantial attack score reductions (e.g., PAIR-1: -58.11) while maintaining low false refusal rates on benign queries
Practical approach enabling training-free database updates without model retraining, addressing real deployment needs
Effective demonstration of adaptability in Table 2, showing performance improves on new attacks without catastrophic forgetting on previous attacks
Novel evaluation framework using operating curves based on FRR budget provides actionable guidance for safety-utility trade-off deployment
Reproducibility supported by promised code/data release and detailed implementation appendices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—the approach is a standard pipeline of existing components (Contriever retrieval, PMI/likelihood reranking, LLM-based extraction/classification) with incremental differentiation from prior RAG defenses (RePD, EDDF, SCR)

Fundamental circular dependency: defense relies on the same LLM (Qwen-2.5-14B) for reasoning about harmfulness through strategy inference, reranking, extraction, and classification, undermining robustness claims if the LLM itself is vulnerable

Methodological concerns with evaluation: (1) benign queries are synthetic and GPT-4o generated, not representing real deployment distributions; (2) suspicious baseline results with IA/SCR achieving 18.85%/13.42% FRR on GPT-4o-mini suggest implementation issues; (3) potential model bias with LLM-generated test attacks matching training distribution
High latency (7.5-22s per sample) makes practical real-time deployment questionable; paper acknowledges but does not adequately address this critical limitation compared to sub-second baselines

Fundamental limitation of retrieval-based defense underexplored: cannot defend against truly novel attacks without database updates, which requires manual identification and curation—claimed 'training-free adaptation' shifts burden rather than solving it

Database construction underspecified: unclear how representative seed queries are, no sensitivity analysis on construction prompts (P_anl, P_gdn, P_ext), and no validation that inferred strategies are accurate or useful

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and success factors: missing error analysis, no case studies demonstrating the extraction/classification pipeline, no statistics on retrieval set composition and relevance

Suspicious baseline comparisons: IA and SCR perform unexpectedly poorly on some models with implausibly high FRR values; baselines may not be fairly configured or represent their intended capabilities

Limited threat model and generalization: English text only, only black-box attacks tested, no evaluation against adversarial attacks specifically designed for retrieval-based defenses, unclear robustness to adaptive attackers

Safety-utility trade-off analysis lacks guidance on realistic FRR budgets; interaction between RAD thresholds and inherent target model alignment not discussed (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B's ≥2.5% minimum FRR)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with strong empirical results across multiple target models, showing substantial attack score reductions (e.g., PAIR-1: 71.45→13.34) while maintaining low false refusal rates
Novel and practical evaluation framework using False Refusal Rate (FRR) budgets and operating curves, providing interpretable characterization of safety-utility tradeoffs
Demonstrated training-free adaptability to new jailbreak strategies through database updates, with clear evidence of no catastrophic forgetting (Table 2) and stability at 500k+ examples (Appendix M)
Well-designed detection-based approach that preserves model utility on general QA tasks (AlpacaEval 2.0, MMLU), unlike competing methods that modify prompts
Clear presentation with comprehensive appendices, good system visualization, extensive ablations on design choices, and promised code release supporting reproducibility
Practical value: training-free updates and tunable safety-utility threshold address genuine deployment requirements
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines established techniques (dense retrieval, LLM classification, voting) in a straightforward manner with main contribution being engineering/application rather than methodological innovation

Database-dependent vulnerabilities: system fundamentally limited by database coverage; no thorough analysis of performance on truly novel attacks or characterization of required coverage; guidance generation relies on potentially unreliable LLM summaries

Evaluation limitations: (1) benign queries are synthetic GPT-4o variants rather than real-world traffic; (2) evaluation confined to StrongREJECT family; (3) text-only, English-only scope; (4) concerning high FRR (>10%) for baseline methods on GPT-4o-mini raises implementation questions
Significant computational overhead: 30-second average latency per query (7.5s extraction step with vLLM) may be prohibitive for real-time applications; no computational cost comparison with baselines

Theoretical understanding gaps: lacks formal analysis of when/why approach works; LLM-based extraction step is probabilistic and opaque; voting scheme lacks theoretical justification; no robustness analysis against adversarial attacks on the defense itself

Reproducibility and scope limitations: depends on OpenAI API for evaluation and database construction; cannot be reproduced without API access; unclear generalization beyond LLM-generated/template-based attacks evaluated
Binary safety-utility tradeoff: tunable threshold enables only block/pass decisions, not nuanced responses or alternative suggestions that users might prefer

Missing critical analyses: no error analysis or failure mode investigation; no comparison against all previous RAG-based methods; limited ablation justifying design choices (K=50, k=10 appear arbitrary)
